content: The document titled Framework for the Evaluation of New Tests for Tuberculosis Infection was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2020. It provides a comprehensive guide for evaluating new diagnostic tests for tuberculosis (TB) infection. The publication is available in both electronic and print formats, with specific ISBNs assigned to each version. The WHO permits the use, adaptation, and redistribution of this work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the document must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that the organization is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The document emphasizes that approximately one-quarter of the global population is estimated to be infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Individuals with this infection are at risk of developing active TB disease, with a lifetime risk of 5–15%, particularly within the first two years following infection. The progression risk varies based on individual factors such as comorbidities, age, and nutritional status. Treating TB infection, also known as tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT), is a critical component of the End TB Strategy (2016–2035). At the 2018 United Nations High-Level Meeting on TB, member states committed to providing TPT to at least 30 million people by 2022, including 6 million people living with HIV (PLHIV), 4 million children under five years old who are household contacts of TB patients, and 20 million other household contacts. Currently, there is no gold-standard method for diagnosing TB infection. WHO recommends the use of either the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) to identify individuals eligible for TPT. tuberculosis, but a positive result does not necessarily indicate the presence of live TB bacteria. Consequently, these tests may remain positive even after successful TPT. While these tests are useful for identifying individuals at higher risk of developing TB, their predictive value for progression from infection to active disease is limited. Less than 10% of individuals with a positive test develop TB disease within two years. Therefore, developing and evaluating tests with higher predictive capacity is a research priority. WHO has published target product profiles for such tests, which should ideally predict the likelihood of TB disease development within two years and provide negative results for individuals who will not progress to active disease. Until new tests with improved predictive performance become available, TST and IGRAs remain the standard diagnostic tools for TB infection. However, in high-burden countries, testing is not mandatory before initiating TPT for high-priority groups, such as PLHIV and household contacts under five years old. For other at-risk populations, testing is recommended to identify those who would benefit most from treatment and to avoid unnecessary medication. These limitations highlight the need for new tests with better operational characteristics. The document outlines a framework for evaluating new immunodiagnostic tests for TB infection. It differentiates between tests for TB infection (e.g., TST and IGRAs) and tests for progression or incipient TB, which aim to predict the transition from infection to active disease. The framework provides guidance on study designs, evaluation protocols, and operational and performance characteristics of new tests. It does not prescribe specific thresholds for analysis or minimum diagnostic performance requirements. The development of the document involved a technical expert group established by WHO in November 2019. This group included members from the WHO Global TB Programme, the New Diagnostics Working Group of the Stop TB Partnership, the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND), and McGill University. The group developed the framework through a series of meetings and a review of previous studies and protocols. The draft was reviewed by an ad hoc expert committee before finalization. The framework emphasizes key considerations for evaluating new TB infection tests, including diagnostic and predictive performance, laboratory characteristics (e.g., sensitivity, precision, reproducibility), safety (for skin tests), costs, and operational characteristics. The document highlights the importance of conducting tests in diverse epidemiological settings and ensuring that study participants represent the populations in which the tests will be used. New tests for TB infection, such as C-Tb, Diaskintest, and ESAT-6-CFP10, as well as simplified IGRA tests like QuantiFERON Access and Standard E TB-feron, are not expected to significantly improve accuracy or predictive ability. However, they may offer operational advantages, such as feasibility in low-resource settings and reduced costs. These aspects are critical considerations in evaluating new tests. The lack of a gold standard for diagnosing TB infection poses challenges for evaluating test performance. WHO has developed a hierarchy of reference standards to assess the evidence base for TB infection tests. Any new test should have predictive performance at least equivalent to existing tests, although achieving significant improvements in predictive ability remains a challenge. Sensitivity and specificity, as well as concordance with existing tests, are important endpoints for comparative studies. It also outlines principles for sample size determination and emphasizes the importance of conducting tests in well-trained settings with adequate supervision and quality control. In summary, the document serves as a comprehensive guide for stakeholders involved in the development, evaluation, and implementation of new TB infection tests. It aims to standardize evaluation processes, promote research, and accelerate the adoption of new tests into global and national policies to support the End TB Strategy and TB elimination efforts.
